newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Israel's Sharansky pays tribute to "guru' Sakharov.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Sharansky pays tribute to "guru' Sakharov.

text.p: Former Soviet dissident Natan Sharansky, now an Israeli minister, on Tuesday paid tribute to Andrei Sakharov, the physicist whose struggle for human rights he said helped bring freedom to Russia.

"He invented the weapon of the word of truth and the struggle for human rights, and he helped prove that it is the most powerful weapon against which no dictatorship can stand," Sharanksy said after visiting Sakharov's grave.
It was Sharansky's first return visit to Russia since he was freed from a KGB jail and turned over to the West in a dramatic prisoner swap ten years ago.
Sharansky, who served nine years on charges of spying for Washington, is now Israel's Minister for Trade and Industry and is leading a trade delegation to Moscow.
Sharansky praised the changes he had seen in Moscow, a city he last saw as the KGB whisked him to prison 20 years ago.

"When I am today in Moscow 20 years after I was arrested in Moscow, I see and feel that even if it looks like the same city, when you talk to people, you see it is a very different country," he told reporters.
"The people enjoy life much more deeply and feel much more security and confidence... The people speak differently, they smell differently, there is no constant self-censorship."
Under a light snowfall, Sharansky laid flowers at Sakharov's simple black tombstone and read from a pocket-size Jewish prayer book. He later visited Moscow's Sakharov Museum.
"With his own example, his own words, he influenced thousands and thousands of poeple and I was one of them," he said. "Sakharov had more influence on my life than anybody else except my wife."

Sakharov, the father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, later became an outspoken critic of the Kremlin's human rights abuses, and was sent into internal exile three years after Sharansky was jailed. He died in 1989, two years before the fall of communism.
Sharansky himself, formerly Anatoly Shcharansky, was one of the most prominent human rights activists of the Soviet era.
His campaigning for Jewish emigration rights was the bane of the KGB, but the spy charges raised against him were regarded in the West as severe even by the standards of the time.
On Thursday, Sharansky is expected to visit the Lefortovo prison where he was held after his arrest. A trip to the labour camp where he served most of his term had been denied, he said.
Sharansky travelled from Israel on Sunday with a group of 60 Israeli businessmen seeking to boost bilateral trade.
Israeli officials say trade between the two countries, virtually non-existent five years ago, is now worth about $500 million a year and expanding fast.
